newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco's trade deficit seen up to 3.0 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: Morocco's trade deficit seen up to 3.0 pct of GDP.

text.p: Morocco, after it devoted 3.2 billion dirhams ($370 million) to wage increases, forecast its trade deficit will rise to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product in 1996/97, up from a previous estimate of 2.7 percent.

Finance Minister Mohamed Kabbaj told reporters in a briefing on Tuesday the government agreed to increase wages in the public sector over a two-year period, starting from July 1996. Morocco has 700,000 civil servants.

Kabbaj said the budget deficit was 5.3 percent in 1995 due mainly to cereal imports after the country was hit by a severe drought. The minister said debt remained the main burden that hampered development of the economy. "For each dirham the state receives from taxes and other receipts, 50 percent would be devoted to pay back the debt," the minister said. The state budget expects 79 billion dirhams in receipts for the fiscal year 1996/97. Morocco has a total foreign debt of $22 billion.
The government changed the fiscal year to run from July 1996 to June 1997, in a referendum last year.
Kabbaj said talks were underway with foreign financial institutions to launch "an international rating of Moroccan debt."

He said that Merrill Lynch and Morgan Stanley would be among the financial institutions to visit Morocco next week for talks on the issue. "Our future plan is to go to the international market... in order to improve our foreign debt," Kabbaj said but declined to give details.
He said he would visit Spain on October 23-24 to negotiate a conversion of Moroccan debt worth $1.3 billion.
"I hope a formula could be found with our Spanish colleagues aimed at a gradual conversion of the Moroccan debt similar to the formula agreed this year with the French government," Kabbaj said.
France accepted the conversion of a Moroccan public debt worth FF1.5 billion earlier this year. It had already converted FF 600 million debt to an equity swap.
The minister said he planned to launch next year a nationwide campaign to mobilise public saving.
"Public saving at present is low at 19 percent of GDP...To be competitive, our economy needs to reach at least 26 percent of GDP," Kabbaj said.
